video_title: Most Economists Get Recessions Wrong feat. Tyler Goodspeed | Ideas Lab | Ep.51
gist: Tyler Goodspeed (Exxon Mobil chief economist, former CEA chair) presents his book 'Recession', built on 132 US and UK recessions back to 1700: expansions never die of old age, the height/speed/duration of a boom carries zero information about the following bust, recessions do not cleanse or reallocate, and monetary/fiscal regime changes show no statistical break in recession depth or duration. He argues recessions come from sector-specific shocks with high linkages and poor near-term substitutes — energy above all — and flags rare-earth export restrictions from China as the shock type most analogous to historical energy, steel and cotton disruptions.

themes.theme: Expansions never die of old age

insights.claim: Using 132 US and UK recessions extended back to 1700, Goodspeed finds an economic expansion is statistically no more likely to end in its 10th year than in its first or second year, on either side of the Atlantic and both before and after 1945.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Positioning that de-risks purely because a cycle is 'late' has no historical base-rate support; expansion age is not a valid recession signal.
insights.quote: economic expansions have never died of old age on either side of the Atlantic, either before or after 1945

insights.claim: Recessions, unlike expansions, DO die of old age: the single strongest predictor of whether a recession ends in the next quarter or year is simply how old that recession already is, true both pre- and post-1945.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Duration-since-onset is a usable timing input for re-risking inside a downturn, in a way that expansion age never is for de-risking.
insights.quote: statistically recessions do die of old age and always have. And in fact the single strongest predictor of whether a recession is going to end in the next quarter or the next year is simply how old the recession is

insights.claim: Goodspeed frames the debate as Peter Pan (expansions never age but can be killed by an external shock) versus the picture of Dorian Gray (hidden excesses accumulate until a reckoning), and concludes the data support Peter Pan.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model for rejecting 'accumulated excess' narratives and refocusing on identifying the shock, not the vintage of the cycle.

insights.claim: The standard post-1945 evidence base of only 12 US recessions is statistically inadequate — quarterly or monthly frequency creates the illusion of degrees of freedom that the 12 cycle observations do not actually provide.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Discount macro research and recession models calibrated only to the postwar US sample; they are fitting a dozen events.
insights.quote: you think that with quarterly or monthly data you have all these statistical degrees of freedom, but you really only have 12

insights.claim: Goodspeed rebuilt the recession chronology using NBER quarterly data back to 1854, annual data to 1790, the Davis and Romer alternative chronologies (because NBER overstates the frequency and duration of pre-1927 US recessions), and colonial American statistics back to 1700.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Earlier findings that pre-1945 expansions died of old age (Diebold and Rudebusch) reverse once the chronology is corrected — the raw NBER series biases long-history cycle work.

insights.claim: Goodspeed began the project believing the 2020 pandemic recession was uniquely exogenous, with no excess or misallocation needing remedy, and concluded from the longer sample that essentially every recession fits that description.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Reframes 2020 from an outlier to the template: exogenous shocks, not endogenous excess, are the normal recession mechanism.

insights.claim: There is no informational content in the height, speed or duration of an economic expansion about the depth, speed, duration or even probability of the recession that follows.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Boom-magnitude indicators (credit growth, investment surges, skyscraper records) should be dropped as recession-severity predictors.
insights.quote: There there's simply not nothing no informational content in the height, speed, or duration of an economic expansion that can tell you anything about the depth, speed, duration, or even probability of the subsequent recession.

insights.claim: The relationship runs only one way: the depth and speed of a recession does predict the height and speed of the subsequent recovery, which Goodspeed summarizes as expansions obeying Newton's third law while recessions perennially violate it.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Deeper drawdowns imply sharper snapbacks — a basis for sizing recovery trades off recession depth rather than off prior boom size.
insights.quote: economic expansions adhere to Newton's third law of motion, uh that to every action there's an equal and opposite reaction, uh whereas economic recessions are perennial violators of Newton's third law

insights.claim: Economies are best modeled as growing close to potential, taking adverse shocks that push them temporarily below trend, then recovering — not as rising above potential and enduring an inevitable corrective overshoot.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Implies output gaps are one-sided; 'overheating' narratives that justify pre-emptive tightening rest on a model the long history does not support.

insights.claim: The policy corollary of the plucking model is that the two things that matter are maximizing the long-run trend growth rate and not obstructing the recovery back to trend — the host's framing, which Goodspeed endorses.
insights.speaker: Kevin Coldiron / Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: A policy scorecard for evaluating administrations: trend-growth measures and non-interference in rebounds, not cycle management.

insights.claim: Goodspeed argues we should worry at least as much about expansions as recessions, since the majority of years economies expand matters more for long-run prosperity than the minority in which they contract — citing that the UK has had far fewer recessions than the US over 200 years yet has long been about 30% poorer.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Fewer recessions is not the objective function; countries optimizing for cycle stability can underperform on level of income.
insights.quote: the UK has had many fewer recessions over the past 200 years than the United States, but the UK is also and has long been about 30% poorer

insights.claim: Goodspeed warns policymakers against 'medicating or sedating' expansions that would otherwise die healthy and innocent, since recessions will happen regardless because history will keep happening.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: A case against pre-emptive cycle-killing tightening; the cost is trend growth and the recession still arrives from an unrelated shock.

themes.theme: Policy regimes barely move the cycle

insights.claim: Goodspeed's findings imply monetary policy matters less than commonly assumed, because recession depth and duration have been remarkably constant across four centuries of radically different monetary regimes.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Supports rule-based over discretionary policy and argues against pricing central-bank skill as a major cycle variable.
insights.quote: I think it would suggest that maybe monetary policy doesn't matter quite as much as we tend to think

insights.claim: Within-cycle macro volatility for GDP, consumption, investment and bank lending has declined since 1945, but only back down to levels that already prevailed before 1914 — making the 1914-1945 period the true outlier rather than the modern era an achievement.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Undercuts the Great Moderation as an institutional accomplishment; volatility regimes may simply mean-revert to a pre-WWI norm.
insights.quote: macroeconomic volatility for GDP, for consumption, for investment, bank lending has declined since 1945, it's actually only declined to levels that prevailed before 1914

insights.claim: Recessions have become less frequent in both the US and UK, but there is no statistically detectable break point at 1913 (founding of the Federal Reserve), 1946 (UK Beveridge reforms), the 1930s New Deal, or the 1960s Great Society — the trend is gradual, not institutional.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Removes the standard justification for crediting central banking or the welfare state with cycle smoothing; look elsewhere for the driver.

insights.claim: The one possible trend break toward longer-lived US expansions Goodspeed identifies is 1785, coinciding with the United States leaving behind colonial-era armed conflict — not any monetary or fiscal institution.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Points to conflict/geopolitical shock frequency, rather than macro policy machinery, as the historical driver of expansion length.
insights.quote: Um there's possibly one exception. And that is 1785 in the United States.

insights.claim: Recession depth has been statistically no different since 1945 than before, and UK recessions have actually been LONGER since 1945 than before, contradicting the expectation that a more interventionist countercyclical state would shorten and shallow downturns.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Automatic stabilizers and discretionary fiscal response should not be modeled as materially reducing drawdown depth in advanced economies.
insights.quote: And if anything, UK recessions have actually been living longer since 1945 than before.

insights.claim: Goodspeed explicitly separates the aggregate result from the normative one: aggregate recovery does not mean every household recovers, so he argues for targeted relief through unemployment insurance including higher replacement rates in high-unemployment conditions, as seen in 2020.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Signals where he expects future policy response to concentrate — transfers and UI rather than broad stimulus or cycle management.
insights.quote: that is not necessarily an argument for inaction

insights.claim: The height, speed and volume of bank credit growth during US and UK expansions does not explain variation in the depth or speed of the bank credit contraction in the following recession.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Credit-gap indicators widely used by macroprudential regulators lack predictive power for the size of the subsequent credit bust on average.

insights.claim: Goodspeed finds UK recovery speed back to 1700 is no different whether or not the recession coincided with a financial crisis, measured both with Stephen Broadberry's binary crisis indicator and with the volume of bank-credit contraction.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Directly challenges the Reinhart-Rogoff prior that post-financial-crisis recoveries are structurally slow, a core assumption in post-crisis growth forecasts.
insights.quote: the speed of of economic recoveries for the United Kingdom going all the way back to 1700 is is no different if that recession involved a financial crisis or not

insights.claim: Mike Bordo of Rutgers found the same result for the United States back to the 1880s — recoveries were no slower when a recession coincided with a financial crisis.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Two independent long-history datasets now contradict the slow-recovery-after-crisis stylized fact for the Anglo-American economies.

insights.claim: Goodspeed reconciles his result with Reinhart and Rogoff's 'This Time Is Different' by arguing their broader country sample introduces correlates — the reasons those countries had crisis-coincident recessions — that are themselves correlated with slow recovery.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Suggests the slow-recovery finding is an emerging-market/institutional-quality selection effect, not a mechanical property of financial crises.

themes.theme: Energy and sector-specific shocks as the real cause

insights.claim: Oil shocks were major contributors to US recessions in 1948, 1953, 1957, 1970, 1973, 1980, 1981, 1990, and — underappreciated — 2001 and 2008.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Energy supply disruption is the single most repeated recession trigger in the postwar US record, including in two downturns usually attributed to other causes.
insights.quote: They were major contributors to US recessions in 1948, '53, '57, '70, '73, '80, '81, '90, and underappreciated 2001 and 2008

insights.claim: Goodspeed distinguishes broad macro shocks that hit all sectors roughly equally (e.g. a pandemic) from sector-specific shocks that hit one or two highly linked sectors whose output is hard to substitute within 12 months — and finds the sector-specific type has been more important historically.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: A screening framework: monitor chokepoint sectors with high input linkages and low short-run substitutability, not just aggregate macro data.
insights.quote: are sector-specific shocks that maybe only directly impact one or two sectors, but those sectors have very high linkages to the rest of the economy

insights.claim: Before oil, industrial action in the coal industry was a perennial recession contributor on both sides of the Atlantic, and further back adverse harvest shocks acted as energy shocks because animal feed (provender) fueled draft-animal transport, while bad UK winters destroyed peat supply used for residential heating and industrial power.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Establishes energy-as-recession-trigger as a 300-year invariant rather than a 1970s artifact, raising the prior on future energy-driven downturns.

insights.claim: The highest-ever price of a barrel of oil or gallon of gas was not the 1973 Arab oil embargo or the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait but June 2008, and overall US energy prices have never been higher since 1945 than in summer 2008.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Reframes the GFC as at least partly an energy shock, which changes what indicators to watch for a repeat.
insights.quote: the highest ever price of a barrel of oil or a gallon of gas uh was not during the Arab oil embargo of 1973 or the Iraqi invasion Kuwait in 1990. It was in June 2008.

insights.claim: By summer 2008 the average American household was spending about $2,000 more per year on energy goods and services than a couple of years earlier, against a backdrop where roughly half of US households have no after-tax savings and energy uses (commuting, school runs, heating, food) are hard to economize on.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Provides a transmission channel — household energy budget squeeze — for translating oil spikes into consumer credit stress.
insights.quote: by summer 2008, the average American household was having to spend $2,000 more per year on energy goods and services

insights.claim: Goodspeed links that energy squeeze directly to the mortgage crisis: by summer 2008 about 5% of American homeowners were seriously delinquent on their mortgage.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Implies mortgage delinquency waves can be triggered by cost-of-living shocks, not only by underwriting quality — a different early-warning set.
insights.quote: by summer 2008, about 5% of American homeowners were seriously delinquent on their mortgage

themes.theme: Banking structure as shock amplifier: US vs UK

insights.claim: The UK's historically lower recession frequency is explained not by temperament but by structure: from 1826 the UK had a nationwide branch banking system, so weakness in one region or sector could be offset by strength elsewhere, like a diversified portfolio.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Banking-system diversification is a first-order determinant of national recession vulnerability — relevant to comparing today's banking structures across countries.
insights.quote: since 1826 in the United Kingdom you had a nationwide system of branch banking

insights.claim: For most of US history until the 1980s, banks could not operate across state lines or even more than one branch within a state, leaving tens of thousands of tiny, undercapitalized, under-diversified institutions that amplified and propagated adverse shocks.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: US recession-proneness was partly a regulatory artifact; the same lens applies to today's regional bank concentration in specific sectors and regions.
insights.quote: not only could you not operate a bank across state lines you couldn't even operate more than one bank branch within a state

insights.claim: The UK's second insulation was fuel mix: it was still coal-intensive when US recessions of 1948, 1953, 1957 and 1970 were oil-driven, and for idiosyncratic reasons went from 1926 to 1972 without a single official coal strike, allowing it to go from a 1947 postwar recession to no recession until 1973.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Illustrates that a country's energy composition, not its policy skill, determined which global shocks it absorbed — a template for assessing today's national exposures.
insights.quote: they went from 1926 to 1972 without a single official coal strike

insights.claim: Goodspeed and the host frame national economies as portfolios with different sector compositions, meaning the analyst's job is less about forecasting recession timing and more about identifying which shock types a given economy is exposed to versus insulated against.
insights.speaker: Kevin Coldiron / Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Reorients macro research toward exposure mapping — a tractable exercise — instead of recession-date forecasting, which the book shows is impossible.

themes.theme: Post-2008 bank regulation as the UK's missing recovery

insights.claim: The UK's failure to return to its pre-2008 growth trend — both a level effect and a rate-of-change effect — is one of the very few exceptions to the plucking pattern across three and a half centuries.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Marks the UK post-2008 experience as a genuine structural break worth explaining rather than a slow cyclical recovery.

insights.claim: Goodspeed attributes it to a post-2008 policy regime change that effectively mandated economies produce with less bank credit — liquidity coverage ratios, supplementary leverage ratios, tiered capital requirements and stress testing — inducing substitution of public-sector lending for private-sector lending.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Frames bank capital and liquidity rules as a permanent negative supply shock to a hard-to-substitute input — a live argument in current deregulation debates.
insights.quote: all of these measures that effectively induced the substitution of lending to the public sector for lending to the private sector

insights.claim: The regulatory shock bit harder in the UK than the US because the UK was historically far more reliant on bank credit for corporate external financing, while the US has a robust venture capital and private equity ecosystem plus thousands of regional relationship lenders.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Non-bank financing depth is a structural buffer against regulatory tightening — a durable US advantage over bank-dependent economies.

insights.claim: The UK has long had fewer but on average bigger banks, so a larger share of its banking system fell inside the scope of the post-2009 regime — a reminder that no policy comes without trade-offs.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Size-threshold regulation binds differently by market structure; concentrated banking systems absorb more of any given rule change.
insights.quote: the United Kingdom has and has long had fewer banks that are on average bigger. And so they were all more likely to be treated by the post-2009 policy regime.

insights.claim: Goodspeed accepts the host's more cynical reading that post-crisis rules pushing banks into sovereign debt resembled financial repression, noting it looks much like how the UK and US worked down their post-WWII debt burdens.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: If today's deficits require captive bank demand, expect regulatory settings that keep banks buying govvies — a persistent bid for sovereign paper and a drag on private credit.
insights.quote: whether it was deliberate or subconscious, I mean it did effectively resemble financial repression

themes.theme: Recessions do not cleanse or reallocate

insights.claim: Goodspeed finds that creative destruction — the movement of people and capital from less to more efficient firms — is impaired rather than enhanced by recessions, despite his own prior wish that recessions served some purpose.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Removes the intellectual case for tolerating downturns as purgative; downturns destroy rather than improve the allocation of resources.
insights.quote: I find that that process is impaired rather than enhanced by recessions

insights.claim: Research and development spending is procyclical — it rises during expansions and falls during recessions — so downturns reduce rather than reallocate innovation investment.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Recessions carry a durable hit to the innovation pipeline, arguing against models where downturns raise future productivity growth.
insights.quote: research and development is procyclical. So, it rises more during economic expansions and then falls during economic recessions

insights.claim: The productivity ladder — workers quitting for better-matched, more productive jobs — collapses in recessions because quits plummet as no one dares leave a job and hiring plummets as firms don't dare take on workers, leaving a period of poor employer-employee matches during and after the downturn.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Quits rate is the mechanism to watch for productivity reallocation; its collapse implies a lingering productivity cost beyond the recession itself.
insights.quote: that whole ladder, that whole productivity ladder, just collapses during economic recessions because quitting plummets, because no one dares to leave a job, and hiring plummets because firms don't dare to take on new workers

insights.claim: Recessions are 'rampant age discriminators' against younger workers and younger, often more dynamic firms — firms that lack physical collateral to pledge and lack a long credit history for bank loans.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Recessions entrench incumbents, implying downturns can be a stagnation mechanism rather than a renewal mechanism — relevant to competitive-moat and small-cap analysis.
insights.quote: recessions are rampant age discriminators. They discriminate against younger workers. They discriminate against younger, often more dynamic firms

insights.claim: Testing reallocation directly, Goodspeed finds the allocation of people and output across sectors at the end of a recovery looks very similar to how it would have looked had the economy continued uninterrupted along trend.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Investors should not expect recessions to accelerate structural rotation between sectors; post-recession sector mix reverts to counterfactual trend.
insights.quote: the allocation, looks pretty darn similar to how it would have looked had it continued uninterrupted along trend

themes.theme: Randomness, base rates and the 2026 risk map

insights.claim: Goodspeed cites Soviet economist Eugen Slutsky, who built a moving-sum series from old Imperial Russian lottery ticket numbers that mapped almost perfectly onto an index of British business conditions over nearly half a century — showing random causes summed together can look cyclical.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Cycle-shaped data is not evidence of a cycle; a warning against cycle-timing models built on apparent periodicity.
insights.quote: It was actually a Soviet economist in Moscow, Eugen Slutsky, who took a bunch of old Imperial Russian lottery tickets and created a moving sum series of the numbers in the lottery tickets.

insights.claim: Goodspeed states plainly that his book demonstrates recessions are unforecastable and unpredictable, but argues the useful response is base-rate updating rather than resignation.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Reframes macro process from point forecasts to conditional probability adjustment around historical unconditional frequencies.
insights.quote: recessions are unforecastable and unpredictable

insights.claim: Goodspeed offers explicit unconditional annual base rates: roughly a 1-in-100 chance of a pandemic-related recession, about 1-in-10 of an energy-related recession in the US (with that probability declining), and about 1-in-50 of a credit-controls-related recession.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Directly usable priors for scenario weighting — and the declining energy number implies less recession risk per barrel of oil shock than history suggests.
insights.quote: In any given year in the United States, there's been about a one in ten uh chance of an energy-related recession

insights.claim: The optimistic finding is that households, businesses and investors have been getting steadily better at absorbing recession-generating shocks since at least 1700, driven mainly by diversification of banking systems and of energy systems both across and within fuels.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Structural shock absorption is improving, arguing for a lower unconditional recession probability going forward than long-history averages imply.
insights.quote: our banking systems generally are are more diversified um than they were previously, in earlier periods. And our energy systems are more diversified both across fuels and and within fuels.

insights.claim: Goodspeed was concerned at the start of the Iran conflict because physical barrels and cubic feet were not flowing into global markets, and said that had the conflict persisted at March-April intensity he finds it hard to see the US or global economy avoiding recession.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Establishes a concrete conditional: sustained physical supply loss at that intensity was, in his view, a recession-grade shock.
insights.quote: if the conflict were to have persisted at the intensity of of say March, April, it it's hard for me to to to see uh the global economy or the US economy not having incurred recession

insights.claim: Four differences make 2026 less oil-fragile than 1973: a dollar of output is far less energy- and oil-intensive, non-core OPEC supply is both a bigger share of the market and more elastic, the energy stack is more diverse, and advanced economies now hold strategic petroleum reserves as a hedge.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Explains observed market resilience to the Iran shock and argues for smaller macro betas to oil spikes than 1970s analogies imply.
insights.quote: a dollar of economic output is today uh much less energy-intensive generally and oil-intensive uh specifically than it was in 1973

insights.claim: The shock Goodspeed thinks is underweighted by others is the threatened Chinese export restrictions on rare-earth elements, currently deferred until the autumn, which he compares to historical energy, steel and cotton supply disruptions with broad spillover effects.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: A named, dated catalyst: rare-earth supply restriction fits his high-linkage, low-substitutability recession template better than macro-level worries.
insights.quote: that's currently deferred until the autumn

insights.claim: Goodspeed argues morally laden crisis narratives with villains, heroes and resolution set in very early — 1772, 1857, 1873, 1929, 2008 — with Bernanke, Paulson and Geithner describing themselves as firefighters, while the actual causes are usually more prosaic.
insights.speaker: Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: A bias check: the dominant story of any crisis forms fast and is usually wrong, so build positions from mechanism rather than narrative.

insights.claim: The economy is described as remarkably robust — a single shock is generally not enough, and it typically takes multiple shocks of different natures hitting around the same time to produce a recession.
insights.speaker: Kevin Coldiron / Tyler Goodspeed
insights.so_what: Sets a high bar for recession calls: look for shock coincidence across unrelated channels, not a single alarming data series.
